Chapter Eight: Drawing from Imagination—Bridging Perception and Creativity.
Once you’ve built up your perceptual skills, something exciting tends to happen. You start wanting to draw things that don’t just exist in front of you, but inside your mind. Drawing from imagination isn’t a totally different skill—it’s really just the next step, building on everything you’ve already learned about seeing and observing. The only real difference? Now, your “subject” is living in your mind’s eye, not sitting on a table or outside your window.
So, how do you actually start drawing from your imagination? Well, it begins with internalizing the visual vocabulary you’ve already picked up from life. The more you draw real objects, the more you fill up your mental library with shapes, forms, spaces, and all those subtle shifts in light and shadow.
Imagine this: you’re picturing a wild landscape, a character from a story, or even just an abstract design. You can reach into that mental library and start piecing together a new image—one that only exists in your mind.
Here’s a simple, practical way to approach imaginative drawing:
First, visualize what you want to draw. Focus on the overall shape and structure—almost like you’re sculpting the idea in your head.
Next, sketch those basic forms lightly on the page. Pay attention to edges and the spaces around your subject, just like you would with a real object.
Picture where the light’s coming from. Add in values to make things feel solid and three-dimensional.
Then, start refining the details, always checking how one part relates to another.
And if you ever feel stuck or unsure, there’s no shame in grabbing a reference—look at a real-life object or photo to help clarify your vision.
This whole process is meant to be playful and flexible. You might bounce back and forth between what you imagine and what you observe. If you’re inventing a creature, for example, you could study animal anatomy for inspiration—mixing reality with imagination to make something new and believable.
Drawing from imagination also invites you to take creative risks. There’s no single “right” answer—just possibilities waiting to be explored. The same skills you’ve honed through observation—patience, openness, and a careful eye—turn into powerful tools for invention and self-expression.
So, the next time you sit down to draw, try letting your imagination take the lead. You might be surprised by what you create.
